title: make pre-push takes too long: the suite runs six times, one process each
description: make pre-push runs tox's whole envlist (black, ruff, pyright and pytest on five Python versions, one after another), then the suite a sixth time for coverage. Measured on 4 cores: fusain's suite takes 173 s per run and oilpaint's 162 s, so pre-push spends 20 minutes or more in each. CI already runs the versions in parallel jobs. Fix: run the tests with pytest-xdist (-n auto) and have pre-push check once, on the current Python (lint env, coverage, wheel, spell-changed); make tox keeps the full matrix.

title: A pen's blots can be turned off, and a light line blots less
description:
Pen.blots: 1 as now (the default: blots stay on), 0 for a pen that never blots, above 1 for a leaky one. It scales what the ball gathers (the drop it lands with and what a turn leaves), independently of Pen.flow, which today is the only control and darkens the line with it.

Also: blots show on the light side of a hatching. The drop the ball can hold (BALL_BLOB * BALL_INK * flow * bound^2) and what it gathers do not depend on pressure in the way the line does, so a faint line gets blobs as big and dark as a firm one's, which reads wrong. What is gathered and left should go with the pressure of the line (measure a blob's darkness against its line's, at light and firm pressure).

Fits with fusain-azn (the ball blots at every point of a gently curving line) and fusain-uoa (a pen in the hand): do the three together. Alters the picture: record the fingerprint and regenerate the images.
close_reason: Pen.blots scales what the ball gathers (0: never blots); what the paper takes of a drop goes with the pressure of the line: the darkest start against its line 2.60 -> 1.87 at pressure 0.15, 1.38 -> 1.36 at 0.9

title: Soft graphite does not smudge: a stump hardly changes a pencil's tone
description: Found measuring graphite for the lake drawing. Every grade has the same binding (0.85), and a stump only moves dust, so rubbing a 2B tone changed it by a few levels and cut its grain by 10 to 15 per cent; an 8B smudged no more than a 4H; nothing could be dragged out onto bare paper. Real soft graphite rubs smooth under a stump or a finger and drags out; hard leads hardly do. Reproduction: s=Sheet(300,120,seed=1); s.shade((10,10,110,110),pencils.B8,0.9); s.smudge([(20,60),(290,60)],tools.STUMP,0.8) left bare paper at x 130..160 at about 219 against 237.
close_reason: Graphite now slides under a tool that smears (slide_graphite in the rubbing kernel): held graphite is pushed from grain to grain and a little comes loose, the more graphite the lead has. One stump pass leaves 82% of a 4H shading's grain, 74% of an HB's, 57% of a 4B's, 34% of an 8B's; set fixative keeps it; erasers and other media are unchanged. Tests in tests/test_dust.py.

title: Coloured pencil: little takes over a light first layer
description: A light wash of coloured pencil (two or three layers at pressure 0.3 to 0.5) waxes the tooth so far that darker pencils laid afterwards hardly show: in the first examples/macaw.py, deep green and blue over a lime wash left it lime. A coloured pencil artist builds ten or more light layers, light to dark. Measure how many light layers the model takes before it resists, against that practice, and recalibrate WAX_FULL and RESIST (and what a light touch lays) if it is too few.
close_reason: Measured, no recalibration. On cartridge paper, light layers (pressure 0.3) of one pencil take 0.80, 0.58, 0.51, 0.39, 0.36, 0.29, 0.25 of the first and fall to a fifth by the tenth: in line with the ten or more light layers of practice. Over three lime layers a dark pencil takes 0.65 of what it takes on bare paper if they were laid at 0.3, 0.41 at 0.5, 0.25 at 0.75 (which polishes the tooth). The first macaw failed because its washes were pressed up to 0.75. A recalibration (WAX_FULL 0.6, wax piling thicker) gained little and broke 'a waxy lead fills the tooth with less than the same lead without its wax'. Pinned by two tests in tests/test_colour.py; advice added to the README and pencils.py.

title: A full tooth takes hardly any more pastel
description: Once the tooth is full, a further stroke of soft pastel lays next to nothing, and a light stroke over it only catches the grain of the strokes before (shop-window reflections came out as plaid; a red coat over a black car came out striped), unless the layer under it is fixed first. A real soft pastel keeps going on over a full tooth for a while: it is opaque and crumbles on top. The agent drawing examples/broadway.py called fix() every few objects to get round it.
close_reason: Measured, no change to the model. On cartridge and on toned grey paper, layers of soft pastel at 0.7 take 0.70, 0.50, 0.36, 0.25, 0.19, 0.12 of the first: the tooth is full after five or six, as on real pastel paper. White over four layers of black reaches a tone of 0.30 (0.64 over one layer), and 0.56 if the black is fixed first: fixing between stages is what a pastellist does. Pinned by two tests in tests/test_fixative.py; advice in the README. Sanded card holding too little is a separate issue.

title: No way to rub or erase an area
description: Sheet.smudge and Sheet.erase take one path. Rubbing a sky or a shadow face smooth means writing a sweep of strokes by hand, with a mask as the pressure. Wanted: an area form, as Sheet.shade is for media: an area (rectangle or polygon), a tool, a pressure that may be a function of (x, y), an angle. Note: a tool keeps its load across a stretch of no pressure, so a sweep through a mask carries dust over the gaps; the area form should lift the tool there. Found by the agent drawing examples/deco.py.

title: Strokes laid with the side of a stick stay speckled when rubbed
description: Two layers of sheet.shade(box, charcoal.VINE, 0.8, 9, tilt=1) followed by two finger passes stay speckled (pixel std 0.158 at mean 0.62); the same with the point rubs smooth (std 0.113 at mean 0.66). A finger should even out the side of a stick as it does the point. Found by the agent drawing examples/deco.py, which avoided tilt for that reason.

title: A firm pencil wears a waxed layer away, stroke by stroke
description: Pressed hard over a waxy layer, a tip drags part of the layer along (burnish). What it still carried when the stroke ended left the paper with it, so many short firm strokes wore the layer away. Found drawing examples/macaw.py. Fix: lay what the tip drags on the marked paper under it where it lifts off (set_down in _engine.py); only off the sheet is it lost.
close_reason: What a polishing tip drags is laid where it lifts off, and it is laid back within a pixel or two (BURNISH_LAY 4), so a firm pencil no longer wears a waxed layer away nor leaves blobs where its strokes end.

title: Tips: wear, tilt, the side of a stick, crayon; graphite shine
description: Step 5 of docs/design.md.
notes: Built: tilt (round points), wear (Stick, a tip whose flat grows with the volume laid; sharpen), crayon and oil pastel (crayons.wax, pastels.oil) with resist depending on what is laid over wax (resist_of), and graphite's shine (Medium.sheen, Sheet.shine, render(gloss=...)). title: The press rework's open choices: what several layers do, how fast unburnished wax comes off an eraser, and its constants
description: Choices made on the conservative side in the rework of press (fusain-2z5, fusain-dq2), each of which the owner may want otherwise. (1) BURNISH and FLATTEN keep their values, so one pass does about what it did (from 0.7 up within a third either way), and results that rested on layers adding up fell: three firm layers of HB flatten 0.34 of the tooth (0.74), 2B 0.16 (0.37), six of HB 0.37 (0.99); four firm layers of coloured pencil polish 0.50 (0.84). If a firm HB should still flatten most of the tooth, FLATTEN has to about double, and one pass then does twice what it did. (2) The level goes by the tip's bearing without the streaks of the lead; with them a stroke left bands polished from 0.2 to 1 and every further pass raised the paper under its hardest bands. (3) The polish level is proportional to how slick the film is: coloured pencil pressed hard in two layers has a gloss of 0.18 (0.37). (4) A dense dark that is not burnished now comes off a vinyl eraser nearly to its stain: four firm layers leave 0.47, 0.18, 0.05 after one, two, three rubs at 0.9 (0.63, 0.42, 0.27 on main), tone 0.46 of the paper's after three (0.10); a burnished one holds as before (0.68, 0.46, 0.32). Its polish is 0.50 where the sum gave 0.84, so it holds as half-toothed wax; if it should hold as before, that is WAX_HOLDS, not the press law. fusain-rz1 was the opposite complaint (an eraser hardly lightened a dense dark). (5) press = crush + polish - crush*polish rather than a maximum or a clipped sum; SETTLE = 2 (1 gave 20 to 50% less in one pass than before, 3 gave 45 to 58% more for dry leads at full pressure); polish capped strictly at wax/WAX_FAST where wax is taken; fixative leaves both. (6) Strokes are 4 to 8% slower in all: 2 to 3% for the second array, 2 to 3% for the law (unprofiled; probably the second firmness per pixel).

title: The hand's +-15% of firmness makes neighbouring strokes differ four-fold in polish near the onset of burnishing
description: What is left of fusain-2z5 once press stops adding up. With ruled strokes a layer polishes evenly (unevenness 0.06 to 0.13); with the hand as hatching has it, one layer of oil pastel at 0.7 is still uneven by 0.63 of its mean. Measured by switching parts of the hand off: as it is 0.63; every stroke as firm 0.47; as firm at its ends too 0.43; each in its place too 0.13. hatching.FIRMNESS (+-15%) at a pressure of 0.7 gives levels from 0.18 to 0.77, a spread of 0.39 of their mean before anything is drawn (0.49 at 0.6, 0.20 at 0.85, about nothing at 1.0), because the onset of burnishing (BURNISH_SOFT, from 0.4 to 0.8) is steep there. It shows in the gloss with the lamp overhead and in how wax holds against an eraser. Needs the owner's view: whether a real hand's strokes differ so in polish (then it is right), whether the onset should be gentler, or whether a hand's firmness should vary less from stroke to stroke than its pressure does within one.

title: The picture depends on NumPy's major version: under NumPy 1.26 every paper's ground differs, and nothing checks it
description: pyproject allows numpy>=1.24, the lock and CI run NumPy 2.5. With Python 3.12, numba 0.68.1 and NumPy 1.26.4, tools/fingerprint.py reports 44 of the 421 recorded marks differing, in all 13 drawings: sheet.ground and what the strokes return in every one, and with them twin/rubbed/pressed/layered/inked/fixed.ground, a stump's _carried, a pencil's wear, one reflectance and one loose. With the same Python and numba and NumPy 2.5.4 all 421 are identical, so it is NumPy's version and not Python's. The likely cause is NumPy 2's promotion rules (NEP 50): a single-precision number times a Python float stays single from 2.0 and was double before, somewhere in how a paper's ground is made (fusain/paper.py, or murex's noise and filters, which oilpaint shares: check there first). examples/stilllife.py has the same dependence in its own code (its direction field is single precision): under 1.26 it draws another picture than the committed one. To decide: require numpy>=2 (simplest, and says what is tested), or make the arithmetic independent of the promotion rules with explicit dtypes and test the oldest NumPy allowed in CI. Found on 15 November 2026 reproducing a review finding on pull request #52.
close_reason: The owner's decision of 15 November 2026: NumPy 1.x is dropped. fusain needs numpy>=2.0 and numba>=0.60 (the first numba that runs on NumPy 2; 0.59.1 cannot be installed with it). With NumPy 2.0.2 and numba 0.60.0, the oldest pair now allowed, all 421 recorded fingerprint marks are as recorded. The numbers that differed are murex's (spectral.srgb_to_reflectance), so murex takes the same requirement in its own pull request.

description: fusain-ck0 put a waxy medium's film on the dust it is drawn over, but all the dust still counts in its way. Over two layers of pale soft pastel a dark coloured pencil shaded at 0.6 leaves the tone at 0.995 of the pastel's (0.968 at 0.9), a crayon at 0.8 at 0.944; since fusain-wo4 a 2B gives 0.65. The bed rule of fusain-wo4 could apply to waxy tips (law[14] is dryness today).

title: What the paper holds fills the tooth for every medium alike: pastel rubbed in takes a pencil poorly
description: A limit of fusain-wo4. Pastel rubbed into the paper takes a pencil only while dust is left on it: a 2B over pastel blended once with a finger is 0.77 as dark as on bare paper, blended again crosswise 0.23; a charcoal pencil over pastel blended once is 0.21, because it takes that ground for one like its own. Dust pressed in keeps no tooth of its own, where fixed dust takes FIXED_ROOM.

title: The macaw's feet: one toe too many lying idle on the branch, two feet that do not read as a pair, wedge claws
description:
examples/macaw.py: after fusain-58g the feet close round the branch, but they still look wrong to the owner's eye ("something's off" about the feet and legs). Two independent critiques of examples/output/macaw.png were then made by fresh agents that were given only the image, with no hint of what to look for; the second also checked against about 30 reference photographs of military and great green macaws (World Parrot Trust, oiseaux-birds.com, iNaturalist). Both found the same faults in the feet. Coordinates are pixels of the 1100 x 1540 image, x then y. Alters one picture: regenerate examples/output/macaw.png.

WHAT BOTH CRITIQUES AGREE ON

1. One toe too many, and it grips nothing. Five digits show on the viewer's side of the perch: (a) one lit grey toe lying along the top of the branch, pointing left, with no claw (about 455-520, 795-815; or 540,800 to 465,820); (b) one long lit grey toe wrapping over the front to the underside (about 530-560, 800-900; claw near 510,915); (c, d) two short dark toes ending halfway down with black claws (about 580-600 and 610-625, y 800-880; claws near 583,880 and 620,876); (e) one long dark toe wrapping to the bottom (about 630-665, 815-900; claw near 635,903). A parrot's foot is zygodactyl, two toes forward and two back, so from the front of a perch at most two toes per foot show, one longer and one shorter, with the other pair hidden behind: four, not five. Critique 1: "The left-pointing toe has no place and does not grip." Critique 2: "A toe lying along the branch belongs to no grip: it is as if that foot pointed left with the body while the others pointed at the viewer."

2. The two feet do not read as a pair. The near foot is pale grey with neat cross-scutes; its neighbours are flat charcoal with none, and the lit near toe changes abruptly to the dark of its neighbours. It is unclear which toe belongs to which foot: the pale foot seems to have one toe too many, or the dark foot does.

WHAT ONE CRITIQUE ADDS

3. Claws (critique 2): straight black wedges pointing down the face of the perch "like fangs". Real claws are long, curved hooks that bite round the wood.

4. Feet against body (critique 2, low confidence on its own): the body is seen from its left side, slightly from the front, yet the toes wrap toward the viewer on a perch running left to right, implying a body turned some 60 to 90 degrees from its feet. Parrots do stand at all angles on a branch; with the toe muddle "it adds to the sense the feet were not worked out". No photograph of this exact pose was found, so this rests partly on reasoning.

5. Toes too long for the perch (critique 1, low confidence): the long toes reach the full half-circumference of a thick branch, longer than a macaw's toes would manage.

6. Where the feet meet the perch (both, under the perch): nothing casts a shadow on the branch, neither the toes nor the body, though the light comes from upper left; the branch is a flat brown fill with mechanical cross-hatching and reads as a dowel.

WHAT WORKS, AND SHOULD BE KEPT

The grey of the feet is right; the scutes on the near toe are well observed; the short tarsus under a feathered "trouser" (the lime lobe at about 455-540, 680-790) is true to parrots; the four wrapping toes are plausibly long outer and short inner on each foot; the feet sit believably under the mass of the bird. Neither critique faulted the legs themselves.

NOTES FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS

- The owner said "feet and legs"; the critiques explain the feet but found nothing wrong with the legs, so ask or look again before calling the legs done.
- fusain-58g was worked from anatomy without reference photographs (the session could not fetch any then). The second critique did fetch photographs: World Parrot Trust, oiseaux-birds.com and iNaturalist answered; Wikimedia Commons rate-limited. Work from photographs of a perched macaw's feet this time.
- The feet come from the solid model in examples/macaw_model.py (toe, feet_blobs, branch_frame, the thighs) and are drawn by draw_feet in both files.
- Changing the model reshuffles every stroke of the bird, because all parts share one random generator: see fusain-ny8, which is worth doing first so that the rest of the picture stays as it is.
- The critiques also ranked other faults of the picture above the feet (the lower mandible, the two-tone green with a dark collar, the untapered and cropped tail, hair-like plumage, blank lores). They are not part of this issue.
close_reason: The feet faced backwards: the branch slanted so that the side we saw was behind the bird, showing the back toes plus a forward toe lying along the top. The branch now slants the other way in depth, so each foot shows its two forward toes wrapping toward us and the back toes are hidden; the two feet are mirror images drawn alike; the claws arch into hooks; the feet cast a soft shadow on the bark; the toes wrap less far. On the owner's eye: the near thigh no longer juts out as a ball, and the near leg comes straight down into the foot, short and stout, without a hump. Owner approved.

title: A crayon line over a tooth full of rubbed charcoal is only half slick to dust
description: The film a crayon lays over dust there is about 0.09 thick against COVERS 0.2, so charcoal from a stick or from a tool still takes at about half rate: in examples/output/crayons.png, third row, the white line goes from 0.60 to 0.40 of the paper's tone where the stump crosses. With drag_film (fusain-pv2) firm crayon layers over dust leave a little less film still. A bug or a design question: how thick a film must be to be slick. Found doing fusain-ma9.

title: A stump has one shallow load: no deep reservoir, and one pass through a tone hardly loads it
description: Left of fusain-9zh. A stump fills slowly and holds only so much (Tool.holds), so that it carries little out of a tone; loaded, it tones bare paper on 6B to 0.72 of the paper's tone where it lands (fusain-6lr had 0.59), a bare stump takes 4.7% of an 8B tone in eight rubs (6lr pinned under 4%), and it can be loaded only by long rubbing or on a scrap of the medium (examples/charcoal.py does that). A second, deep reservoir that fills and empties slowly (a stump used for long stays grey) is not modelled; if one quick pass through a dark tone should load a stump noticeably, that is a further change.

title: A flat end on a hook shorter than half the tip cuts into the stroke before the bend
description: lay_stroke / within_ends: the heading of a flat end comes from the last two samples, and every tip position within a tip's reach of the end is cut by that line. A flat stroke 24 wide along y=80 turning square up for 2 to 6 px: the inside half of the stroke 4 to 12 px before the corner is 0.53 to 0.87 of the outside half (should be 1 or more; 0.44 at width 12, hook 2), and 10 to 42 pixel-passes are left past the cut. A last leg of half a tip or more, and a smooth sharp curve, are fine and tested. Pinned by three non-strict xfails: tests/test_strokes.py::test_a_flat_end_on_a_short_hook_leaves_the_stroke_before_it_whole. Found doing fusain-wxf.
close_reason: A flat end's cut takes what lies beyond the stroke, not the stroke: past the line across the end, a pixel stays as far as it is in the band the tip's flat sweeps along the path (within half the flat of the path at a sample within reach of that end, behind the line across the path there). One formula for every flat end, no threshold: strokes with no short hook are laid to the bit as before, and from a hook of one sample spacing to half a tip the cut crosses less and less of the band. Width 24, hooks 2, 4, 6: inside against outside before the corner 0.66, 0.53, 0.87 -> 1.19, 1.29, 1.34; over 160 strokes (widths 6 to 48, both ends, both turns) the band before the bend is bit-identical to the round-ended stroke's. The three xfails are plain tests, with 32 more cases. Left: the band is taken to the tip's flat, half a pixel inside its antialiased rim (the outermost row has 0.60-0.69 of the round stroke's), and it ends at the last sample before the corner, up to a spacing short of it.

title: Dust a film has set stays set after the film is worked away
description: bonded[SET] does not record whether fixative or a film set the dust. When a firm pass presses a film into the tooth (fusain-pv2), the dust it bound stays set and on top of it. Over coloured dust this dulls the result: red crayon over blue pastel goes from chroma 5.6 to 4.0 after the blender.

title: A layer is one mixture, so a film cannot be told from the dust it lies on
description: What is set, film and paste are stored as volumes within a dust layer of one composition. A tool, or a firm tip (fusain-pv2), that takes a film takes the layer's average colour: a dark film on white dust carries white with it, so one firm pass of the blender moves only 0.21 of the dark where more of the film's own pigment should go.
notes: From fusain-wo4: a film laid on a film should join it on top, not bury it. A 6B at full pressure over pale pastel goes 0.24, 0.29, 0.31 of the pastel's tone over three layers (lighter each time), and a 2B at 0.6 levels off at 0.43 where on bare paper it reaches 0.11. Also: the rule that a film with no wax comes away with the dust it lies on is a yes/no test on wax at the pixel; a pencil film at a pixel that also carries wax is treated as a wax film; and stir_up does not stir a dry film that later dust has buried.

title: Press grows with every pass, so a shading polishes in streaks where its strokes overlap
description: press is summed pass by pass up to 1. With no threshold at all (polish in proportion to pressure), one layer of oil pastel at 0.7 is still polished unevenly from stroke to stroke, about 0.6 of its mean, and 0.55 even at full pressure: the hand's overlaps, stray and +-15% firmness. A pressure flattens wax and fibres to a level set by the load, not by how often it is pressed; press approaching a level set by the bearing would even it out. It shows in the gloss with the lamp overhead, in how wax holds against an eraser, and in the relief. Found doing fusain-bre, whose soft onset took the unevenness from 0.78 to 0.58 (coloured pencil at 0.6) and could do no more.
close_reason: Press no longer adds up. A tip of firmness f has a load (BURNISH*f on wax, law[10]*f on paper: what a pass used to add); the level is min(load, 1), times how slick the film is for polish; below it each part of a pass closes SETTLE*max(load,1)*passing of the gap (SETTLE = 2), at or above it nothing changes. The level goes by the tip's bearing without the streaks of the lead. A blender at 0.7 passed 1, 2, 3, 6 times: 0.40/0.66/0.87/0.96 before, 0.29/0.37/0.40/0.41 now (level 0.42); a lighter pass over a firmer one changes nothing, a firmer over a lighter raises it. Ruled strokes (hand=0) polish a layer evenly: oil pastel at 0.7 0.418 to 0.120, coloured pencil 0.353 to 0.128. With the natural hand the unevenness is nearly what it was (oil pastel one layer at 0.7: 0.649 to 0.631; two crossed layers at 0.6: 0.735 to 0.565): it is the hand's, +-15% of firmness meeting the steep onset of burnishing, and is filed apart. Strokes 2 to 3% slower for the law.

title: A light ballpoint line's blob is as wide as a firm line's
description: blot's radius is BLOB_WIDE * (radius + 0.5) at any pressure, while a light line is narrower. Since fusain-43t the volume of a blob follows the pressure of the line, but its width does not.
close_reason: A blob is BLOB_WIDE times as wide as the disc of the ball that comes down to the peaks of the tooth, the rule roll_over has where the ball lands: on cartridge paper a 6-pixel pen's blob is 3.12, 3.67, 3.99, 4.18 and 4.18 in radius at 0.05, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.9, where it was 4.18 at all of them. The disc is full from about 0.41 on cartridge paper, so above that the blob no longer widens while the line still does a little.

title: A ballpoint drop inks all of a pixel that holds a pass of ink, however small the drop
description: blot sets inked = max(inked, min(total ink / full, 1)) from the pixel's total ink, not the drop's. So any drop, however small, makes a partly inked pixel of a heavy line fully inked and closes its white specks. This is what moved pixels by up to half their tone when the invisible drops of a gently curving line went (fusain-azn).
close_reason: A drop adds to how much of a pixel is inked the share of its bare paper that the drop itself would cover a firm pass thick (inked += (1 - inked) * min(dv / full, 1)), as a tool's dust does on cover: a drop of a billionth of a pass leaves a heavy line's edge 0.503 bare, where it took it to 0.337.

title: Sheet.rub draws a seed for each stretch it rubs, so where its pressure is zero shifts every later mark's grain
description: rub() splits each pass into runs where pressure > 0 and calls _rub once per run, and each call draws an integer from sheet._rng. So the number of draws depends on the zeros of the pressure field: a drawing whose rub pressure comes from what it measured, or that is changed slightly, re-seeds every stroke after it, and the whole picture's grain changes. Drawing one seed per pass, or per rub, and deriving the runs' seeds from it would make the sheet's random sequence independent of the pressure. examples/lake.py works around it with a pressure floor (LIGHTEST_RUB). Found doing fusain-098.
close_reason: A rub draws one seed from the sheet's generator, after its checks and whatever its pressure; each run has a seed derived from it by integer arithmetic (the sample of the rub it starts at, times an odd step). Tests pin that five pressures with other zeros leave the generator in the same state and what is drawn after the same. examples/lake.py no longer needs LIGHTEST_RUB.

title: Strokes and rubs twice as fast again, with documented numba options only
description:
The private options _nrt=False and forceinline=True were taken out (the user does not want fusain to rely on undocumented options); inline="always" is in their place. That costs a factor of 1.4 to 2.0 on strokes and 1.2 to 1.8 on rubs against the private options (1120x820: HB 1.48 -> 2.37 s, finger rub 1.97 -> 3.52 s, stump 3.55 -> 4.41 s, 2000 short strokes 0.41 -> 0.78 s).

The cost is numba counting a reference to each array a kernel passes to a helper, per pixel. Win it back with public options only: fold the per-pixel helpers into their kernels by hand, or pass them numbers (or one packed row) and not arrays, or hoist what they read out of the pixel loop. Measure with tools/benchmark.py; the fingerprint must stay identical. Mind ruff's complexity cap of 13 and that _engine.py stays readable. Also measure the cold compile time, which inline="always" may have lengthened.
notes: From the rubbing lane (fusain-9zh, 9i8): per-pixel helpers of rub_under that are given the tool's arrays cost time. Twice there: lay_load as an @_inlined helper cost about 15% of a rub until it was folded by hand, and the wax bookkeeping in lift about 20% until it was guarded. A single rub pass is a tenth to a sixth slower than before that lane; lift, lift_bonded, spread_dust and spread_top are worth folding by hand and measuring. From the stroke lane: slide_on wraps bear (one more call per step). From fusain-wo4: one more array passed to two per-pixel inlined helpers (reach_under, spread_top) cost a tenth of every rub until they were given numbers instead; rubbing charcoal is about a seventh slower than before that lane (half because compressed over vine now has films in it). A convention worth writing into AGENTS.md once measured: a per-pixel inlined helper is given the numbers it needs, not one more array.
close_reason: Strokes and rubs are at or below what the private numba options gave, with documented options only: no kernel counts a reference to an array as it works (tools/refcounts.py, tests/test_refcounts.py hold it there). Sheet of 1120 by 820, seconds, before -> after: shade HB 2.90 -> 1.48; soft pastel 2.07 -> 1.04; coloured pencil 3.70 -> 1.81; finger rub 6.68 -> 2.42; stump rub 7.43 -> 3.28; kneaded eraser 6.14 -> 1.13; 2000 short strokes 0.79 -> 0.43; render 1.00 -> 0.54. Recorded and thorough fingerprints (325 drawings, 10327 marks) identical, every example image byte for byte. Cold compile 18.3 s -> 19.2 s.

title: Faster strokes at the cost of the picture
description: What fusain-14p left because it would change the picture (rough estimates): tip steps of width/4 instead of width/8, about 1.8x on stroke and rub kernels; laying once per pixel per stroke instead of about nine times, 3 to 4x on the stroke kernel; a cheaper reach curve than pow(x, 0.6), about 10%; pigment stored by id instead of 24 bands per layer, rubs 2x or more and about 6x less memory, but a different mixing model; threads over tiles in a fixed order. Still exact and not done: fold the gathers and the blend of a render into the kernels (about 25% of a render); vectorise the per-row geometry pass (10 to 15% of a stroke). Also: examples/stilllife.py spends about 80 of its 82 s in its own planning code.
notes:
Done, with no change to the picture: examples/stilllife.py plans in half the time (67 s -> 31 to 35 s; the cloth's folds in a compiled kernel, only the cells with a target weighed); the gathers and the blend of a render are in two kernels (thicken, show_through: render 1.00 s -> 0.54 s, with fusain-95m). Tried and not taken: vectorising the per-row geometry pass. The first loop vectorises (fingerprint identical) but saves 0.04 s of an HB shade, below the noise: rows are 7 to 8 pixels for a width-6 tip, and the streak lookup and the jitter hash stay scalar. What is left here changes the picture and needs a decision: tip steps of width/4, laying once per pixel per stroke, a cheaper reach curve (pow(x, 0.6) is about 11% of a stroke; graphite ** 5 in slip_of is paid at every pixel a stump rubs over graphite), pigment stored by id, threads over tiles. Where an HB shade's 1.4 s goes after fusain-95m: laying and settling about 0.8 s, per-row geometry 0.3 s, the reach curve 0.16 s, Python and per-step overhead 0.14 s.

Measured 2026-11-17 (processor time, best of 5, against main, AVX-512 and haswell alike). Profile of an HB shade, 1.50 s: overhead 0.10, geometry 0.19, reach pow 0.36, laying 0.65, settling 0.20; graphite**5 is 11% of a stump's rub. Prototypes: width/4 steps for strokes and pens, rubs kept at width/8: shades 1.7-1.9x, pens and short strokes 1.45x; mean L* -0.14 (HB) to -0.48 (4B and vine at full pressure), grain +0.1-0.4 sigma, no pattern in the change; worn sticks wear a little wider. Width/4 for rubs too: rubs 1.8-2.05x, but rubs bead along every pass (finger on vine: 68% of pixels move >1 L*) and the stump-streak test fails. Reach curve from a table plus graphite**5 as products: shades 1.07-1.2x, stump 1.09x, at most 0.005 L* anywhere. Width/4 for strokes plus the table: shades 1.9-2.0x, short strokes and pens 1.5x, stump 1.1-1.2x. Not prototyped: lay once per pixel (about 1.4x on top), pigment by id, threads over tiles. Report with image diffs: https://claude.ai/artifact/K5DVxZk9i9yU1UA952Seb8
Owner's choice, 2026-11-17: width/4 steps for strokes and pens, with the reach table (PR #74). Rejected, not to be proposed again: width/4 steps for rubs (rubs 1.8-2.05x, but beads along every pass of a rub: finger on vine 68% of pixels moved >1 L*, stump streaks below the test); pigment stored by id (a different mixing model, every mixture changes; 300 of a 1120x820 sheet's 349 MB are bands; very large, partly in murex); threads over tiles (no processor time saved, wall clock up to about 3x on 4 cores; seams, and wear and drag along a stroke no longer add up). Left open, not rejected: lay once per pixel per stroke (laying is 43% of a shade; about 1.4x more on top of width/4, picture cost unknown until prototyped). Also measured, 6 steps per width: shades 1.4-1.55x, half the ripple.
close_reason: Strokes twice as fast, as the owner chose: strokes and pens step a quarter of the tip's width (an eighth before), the reach curve is read off a table and graphite**5 is worked out by products. Shading 1.9-2.1x (AVX-512 and haswell), short strokes and pens 1.5x, a stump's rub 1.1-1.2x. The picture: tone 0.14-0.5 L* darker where the paper fills up (wax crayon 0.5-0.7 lighter), grain a little coarser, a ripple of 2% along lines on paper with no tooth, a pencil film over pastel 0.77-0.80 of the line (0.88-0.90 before). Rubs and the stylus keep an eighth. Also fixed: a NaN under an eraser that drags wax. Rejected candidates and the one left open are in the notes.

title: Move to murex: dense points of a Path computed once, and a compiled km_layer over a ground per pixel
description: Found doing fusain-14p. (1) A murex Path recomputes its dense points on every call (sample() and length each call _dense()); fusain works around it with sheet._Dense, through the _dense subclass hook. Path sampling is about 0.4 ms a stroke and dominates short strokes (37,000 strokes in lake.py: about 15 s); compiling the spline sampling would help. (2) km_layer has no compiled path for a ground per pixel (_km_layer_batch takes one ground), so fusain carries its own copy (km_depth, km_over in _engine.py), pinned bit for bit to sp.km_layer by tests/test_exact.py. Both belong in murex; a change to murex's numbers is a breaking change there and oilpaint must be checked.
close_reason: murex 0.2.0 has both; fusain requires it and its _Dense is gone

title: The ball blots at every point of a gently curving line
description: roll_stroke calls blot whenever drop > 1e-9, which a tiny turn satisfies, so nearly every step lays an invisible drop: about 29% of the pen's time. A threshold tied to what shows would change pictures slightly and take about 25% off the pen kernel.
close_reason: A drop stays on the rim until the line has turned far enough to show (BALL_SHOWS); hatching 0.350 -> 0.286 s, pen over graphite 0.492 -> 0.329 s; nothing is lost

title: An eraser does not smear wax, and coloured pencil leaves no stain
description: In life a vinyl eraser smears a burnished dark and always leaves a tint. In the model the last of a light layer comes off cleanly and nothing is smeared. Also: a white or light pencil pressed hard burnishes only as an ordinary pencil (Medium.melts is 1 for the blender only), and the knife does not touch ballpoint ink.
close_reason: A vinyl eraser smears dense or burnished wax along its way (near-black, burnished: dE 15.4 at one tool width, 2.6 at six to nine; was 0); wax leaves a stain no rubber eraser takes (STAIN: a light near-black layer on cartridge ends at 0.873 of the paper's tone after four rubs, was 1.000); a white or pale pencil burnishes nearly as the blender (pencils.melts_of: white 0.75, strong colours 0) and lightens; a knife or a sand eraser takes ballpoint ink with the paper (a knife line on firm hatching goes back to 0.98 of the paper's tone).

title: Erasing or scraping polished wax leaves press as it was
description: The tooth stays level after the wax that levelled it is gone (eraser, tools.KNIFE, tools.SAND_ERASER), so what is drawn there next touches the whole pixel.
close_reason: Where a pixel holds wax its press is the wax's polish: as a tool thins the wax below WAX_FAST the press it held up goes, and a sand eraser or a knife cuts the paper and takes a dry tip's crush with it. Burnished coloured pencil scraped by a knife: press 0.996 -> 0.000, a light HB over it touches 0.638 of the pixels (was 0.998; fresh paper 0.679); a vinyl eraser leaves burnished wax and its press (0.991).

title: Under the default lamp the gloss of polished wax greys burnished darks, patchily
description: WAX_SHEEN 0.025 at about 0.9 of the lobe adds about +10 L to a burnished black (L 9 to 19), and it follows the unevenness of press stroke by stroke. examples/macaw.py is rendered with gloss=0 to avoid it. Related: the burnish threshold makes press patchy.
close_reason: The gloss of wax is narrow (WAX_SHININESS 5 -> 80): a burnished black under the default lamp L* 18.1 -> 10.3 (matte 6.8), as glossy as before with the lamp overhead; examples/macaw.py is rendered with its gloss again

title: Examples that look at the sheet redraw on any engine change
description: examples/lake.py and the like measure the sheet as they draw, so a tone change of a few thousandths gives a different drawing (different trees), which makes before/after comparison of those pictures noisy. Make them deterministic against small tone changes (e.g. calibrate on a scratch sheet, quantise the feedback).
close_reason: examples/lake.py was the only example steered by what it saw; marks are now scattered over fixed places and fade in with the need, so a tone change of 0.3% moves 0.001% of pixels by more than 8/255 (was 18%)

title: A flattened patch keeps pits in its relief
description: press means level with the peaks, so valleys the lead never reached stay at their old depth beside a plateau in surface_height. In life the peaks come down towards the valleys.
close_reason: surface_height is tooth * (1 - press): a pressed patch is level with its valleys. Six firm layers of 4H: spread of heights 0.210 -> 0.029, pits deeper than a quarter of a tooth 6.3% -> none

title: The burnish threshold makes press patchy
description: press is raised only above a pressure of 0.6, so around 0.6 to 0.75 some strokes cross the threshold and others do not. Wax gloss now shows it as faint streaks, e.g. in the navy oil-pastel ground of examples/output/crayons.png. Squaring press in the gloss mitigates it; a soft onset is the proper fix.
close_reason: Polish and flattening set in by degrees from a pressure of 0.4 (firmness, BURNISH_SOFT), exactly the old law from 0.8: unevenness of press on two crossed layers at 0.6, dark coloured pencil 0.78 -> 0.58, oil pastel 1.08 -> 0.73; firm pressure does what it did

title: A tip narrower than a groove skips it
description: A fine point drawn along an indented line (Sheet.dent) should follow it down, but the model does not know the groove's width, so every stick is treated as riding on the paper either side. Found doing fusain-dyh.
close_reason: A tip rests on the highest of the paper it covers, so a point narrower than a groove goes down into it (an HB point 1 px wide lays 0.75 of its line on the floor of a 3 px groove, from 0) and a broad tip still rides over; the floor of a groove bites as a flattened tooth.

title: A pen in the hand: gathered ink carries from stroke to stroke
description: The blob where a ballpoint lands is a random draw per stroke, not what the previous stroke gathered. A pen in the hand, as Stick is for a medium and Smudger for a tool, would carry the gathered ink over. Also: black ink bronzes grey, where a real black ballpoint bronzes violet or copper.
close_reason: HeldPen keeps the ink its ball gathers from stroke to stroke, until wipe(); ink is conserved; Pen.bronze, and black ink bronzes as its violet does

description: lay_stroke now gives the paper under the tip where it lands and lifts what it would have had if the tip had slid on and off (put_down, fusain-lgg). rub_stroke (stumps, fingers, erasers) and roll_stroke (ballpoint) still have the old ramp: half strength at the end of a path, fading over a tip width. Also untested: a flat end on a sharply curving end of a path.
notes: The ballpoint half is done (roll_stroke: ink half a pixel behind the landing 0.28 -> 1.04 of the middle's; a dot is 0.91 to 1.0 as dark as a line, from 0.09). Left: rub_stroke, and the test of a flat end on a sharply curving end of a path.

The flat end on a sharply curving end is tested: fine but for a hook shorter than half the tip (filed).

title: The side of a stick bears evenly across its length
description: A stick on its side still marks with an elliptical footprint, so the band fades towards its edges, where a real flat stick of charcoal or pastel lies even across its length. Found doing fusain-3z1.
close_reason: Medium.flat_side: a stick of charcoal, pastel or crayon laid flat bears like a stadium, even across its band and cut straight where it lands and lifts (share of the band at 0.9 of its middle or more: 0.43 -> 0.92; an edge falls over 3.5 rows, from 23.5); a pencil's side keeps its soft ellipse. Sheet.shade lays such bands side by side.

title: The wax of smeared oil pastel paste stays where it was laid
description: held[IW] counts the wax at a pixel wherever it lies. When a finger moves oil pastel paste (Sheet.paste) the wax does not follow: the smear is not slick and the place it left stays slick.
close_reason: Wax leaves a pixel with what it is in, rides on the tool (Smudger.wax) and comes down with the paste: the smear of three layers of oil pastel carries 0.297 of its volume in wax (was none) and charcoal over it takes 0.034 of what bare paper takes (was 0.32); wax on sheet plus tool is conserved.

title: Burnishing does not drag a film that lies over dust
description: burnish() polishes and drags only held; a film (Sheet.film, a waxy medium laid over dust) in the two layers is neither smeared along nor laid into the valleys by a firm pass.
close_reason: A firm tip drags a film in the two layers by the share it drags the wax the paper holds, and lays it into the tooth: share of a dark film over pale pastel worked into the tooth by one firm pass of the blender 0.01 -> 0.21; pigment and wax conserved.

title: A pencil line drawn over pastel dust shows under it
description: The held share of a dry medium (graphite, charcoal pencil) goes in the tooth, under the dust, so a graphite line over a light opaque pastel shows only as a ghost. fusain-ck0 fixed this for waxy media only (Sheet.film); extending the rule to dry media would put most of a second graphite layer on the first one's dust and break the graphite calibrations, so it needs its own design.
close_reason: A dry medium lies on a bed of dust: dust beyond the crumbs its own mark would have is a bed; the tip rides on it, its held share is a film on the dust (no wax, binds nothing), and the bed takes no room in the tooth. A 2B line over two layers of pale soft pastel lays 0.78 of what it lays on bare paper and is 0.80 as dark (was 0.02 and 0.01); over fixed pastel 0.79 / 0.81. Graphite on graphite is unchanged to the bit (thorough fingerprint). Where a pixel has no wax a tool lifts such a film as it lifts the dust it lies on: a kneaded eraser takes 0.79 of the line on loose pastel, 0.26 on bare paper, 0.25 on fixed pastel.

title: A stump lays dust on wax as on paper
description: rub_stroke lays what a tool carries on any pixel, waxed or not. Charcoal smeared across a crayon line greys it, where on wax it would hardly cling. Visible in the third row of examples/output/crayons.png where the stump crosses the crayon lines. Found fixing fusain-8nq.
close_reason: Wax refuses the dust a tool brings as it does a dry stick's, and what it refuses stays on the tool: a charcoal-loaded stump across one firm crayon line leaves on it 0.12 of what the paper beside takes (was 0.97). A tool no longer stirs or lifts loose dust through a film.

title: A finger carries dust too far: a rubbed join of two pastels is one flat mix
description: Found doing fusain-6lr, once a tool in the hand (Smudger) kept its load. Rubbing a finger to and fro across the join of an orange and a blue soft pastel (examples/colour.py, examples/fixative.py, the same with oil pastel in examples/crayons.py) gives one even olive over the whole width rubbed, with no passage from one colour to the other: tried at pressures 0.3 to 0.6, 9 to 36 passes, passes 44 to 110 px long with a finger 22 wide, all flat. In examples/broadway.py a finger rubbed to and fro over the far fronts and the sky brought the colour of the fronts all over the sky (worked around: pulls from the sky down, with a bare finger). Cause: where it bears a tool lifts about two thirds of the loose dust in a pass into its load, and lays the load back so slowly that it travels far: a loaded 10 px stump on bare paper leaves a trail whose pigment halves every 40 px (4 widths), and a finger carries a colour 2 to 4 of its widths. A real finger smears most of the dust within a fraction of its width and carries only a small share further, so a rubbed join is a gradient a width or two wide. Wanted: most of what is lifted laid back close by (the dust on the face of the tool, as spread_dust does), a small share carried far; judged by the width of the gradient across a rubbed join, and by the trail of a stump dragged out of a tone (tests/test_dust.py pins that one). Related and not modelled either: a stump that has been used for long stays grey and tones lightly for a long time; here one load is spent in about twenty widths.
close_reason: A tool carries little far: most of what it moves is the dust on its face, laid back within a few pixels; it holds only so much (Tool.holds), lifts little per pass, and gives its load to bare tooth only. A rubbed join of two soft pastels is a passage 1.4 finger widths wide (was 5.5, all that was rubbed); a stump dragged out of vine charcoal drags out 8 columns of tone (was 20); loaded on 6B it tones bare paper to 0.72 of the paper's tone where it lands and lays 0.95 of its load in 28 widths.

title: A stump or finger starts every pass clean
description: Found drawing examples/lake.py. Each Sheet.smudge pass, and each pass of Sheet.rub, starts with a tool that carries nothing and takes what it lifted away with it at the end. So: (1) where a pass lands on a tone it lifts a pale dot, visible as dotted rows along the edge of a rubbed area; (2) rubbing a dark tone many times lightens it steadily (about 200 overlapping finger drags through a reflection took it from 124 to 198), where a real stump is soon loaded and gives back as much as it takes; (3) a loaded stump cannot be used to draw a pale tone on bare paper, which is a standard pencil technique. Wanted: a tool in the hand that keeps its load from pass to pass (as Stick is a medium in the hand), cleaned on request; Sheet.rub should carry the load across its own passes. Reproduction of (2): s=Sheet(300,120,seed=1); s.shade((10,10,290,110),pencils.B8,0.9); s.rub((10,10,290,110),tools.STUMP,0.9) several times and compare the tone.
close_reason: Smudger: a tool in the hand keeps its load from pass to pass; Sheet.rub carries the load across its passes

title: A paper texture between wove and rough: a pebbled tooth for charcoal
description: Found redoing examples/deco.py on a paper without the laid pattern. A real charcoal paper has a pebbled or honeycomb tooth: irregular pits a few pixels across, varying from pit to pit. 'wove' removes all variation larger than about 1.5x the grain, so it reads as fine fibres and a rubbed tone looks salt-and-pepper when enlarged. 'rough' keeps the large-scale variation (it has no equivalent of _no_broad), so at small grain it goes blotchy, like camouflage. Wanted: a texture that keeps only the medium scale (band-passed), usable at grain 3 to 5. Judge on flat charcoal tones and gradients, enlarged.
close_reason: Added the pebbled texture and papers.CHARCOAL

title: Sanded card holds little more pastel than cartridge paper

A real sanded paper takes many more layers than an ordinary one (ten or more against three or four). The room in the tooth depends on depth and bite only, and raising the depth also makes the paper grainier; sanded card may need a way to hold more without being deeper.

title: Ballpoint: blobs of ink and the sheen of heavy ink

The groove the ball presses into the paper is fusain-dyh.

A firm pencil does not flatten the tooth (so graphite's shine still glints on the grain), and there is no way to indent a line below the surface, as a stylus or a ballpoint does, for a pencil shaded over it to skip. Needs a depth-below-surface field, separate from press.

title: A kneaded eraser lifts oil pastel like dust
description: The share of an oil pastel that the paper does not hold at once lies in the dust layers, so a kneaded eraser lifts it as it lifts charcoal. A real oil pastel smears under a finger but does not come off on a kneaded eraser; it has to be scraped.
close_reason: What the paper does not hold of an oil pastel is paste: a kneaded eraser lifts 19% of a layer, down from 53%.

title: Charcoal over one firm crayon line still greys it
description: A single firm line of wax crayon lays a film of wax thinner than WAX_FULL, so it is not yet as slick as it gets, and it is pressed level, so charcoal dust lies over all of it: charcoal shaded over the line leaves it as dark as the grainy paper around it. Wax resist with dry media therefore does not show for single lines (it does over three firm layers: tests/test_crayons.py).
close_reason: Wax is fully slick to a dry medium once it covers the tooth: charcoal takes 8% on one firm line, down from 39%.

title: The side of a stick is as wide for every medium
description: A stick held on its side marks a band five times the width of its point (SIDE in _engine.py), whatever it is. That suits a pencil lead; a long stick of charcoal or pastel laid flat marks a band as wide as the stick is long. Let the medium or the Stick say how long its side is.
close_reason: Medium.side and Stick(side=) say how long the side of a stick is.

title: A held medium laid over dust ends up under it
description: The held layer is always rendered under the two dust layers. A coloured pencil or a crayon drawn over pastel or charcoal dust therefore shows under the dust, where in life it lies over it and partly binds it.
close_reason: A waxy medium laid over dust now lies on it as a film and binds part of it. Dry held media are not covered: filed separately.

title: Make strokes faster
description: Shading 1120x820 pixels with an HB of width 6 takes about 2.4 s (2.1 s before colour was added). The time is in lay_stroke's work per pixel under the tip: each pixel is visited by about nine steps of the tip, and each visit hashes three numbers, takes a power and a square root, and loops over the 24 bands. Ideas: a table of the streaks per pass, the jitter once per pixel, fewer steps for wide tips. The drawing must stay byte-identical (tools: a fingerprint of held, under, loose, cover and press).
close_reason: Strokes 1.5 to 2.3 times as fast, rubs and renders 1.8 to 2.9, byte-identical (tools/fingerprint.py). Further gains need the picture to change or work in murex.

title: Calibrate graphite tones against scans of real pencil
description: The constants of fusain/_engine.py were set so that tones land near figures estimated from experience (docs/design.md, One step of a stroke), not measured. Scan swatches of real 4H, HB, 2B and 6B on cartridge paper at a few pressures and numbers of layers, and fit the constants to them.

title: Polish can exceed what the wax holds by up to 0.004 until the next lift, and a melting tip can polish a pixel where it lays no wax
description: Two small leaks in polish going with the wax (fusain-dq2). (1) In rub_under, wax can leave a pixel after bare_tooth has run in the same visit (push_along's drag, spread_top), and cover can rise after it: polish then exceeds wax / covered / WAX_FAST by up to 0.004 until a tool next lifts there. Calling bare_tooth after push_along would close most of it; the order of rub_under was left alone. (2) A melting tip can raise polish on a pixel where it lays no wax (a tooth full of a dry medium): that polish has no wax to go with and stays. Older than the rework (it was press then). Also seen: the burnished dark's gloss varies a little more from place to place than it did (L* added, blurred by 2: 0.115 to 0.226), because seams where only the blender's rim passed stay below a polish of 1 where the sum saturated everything.
close_reason: Polish goes with the wax wherever a tool or a tip leaves. rub_under: bare_tooth runs last in each visit and caps polish at what the wax left holds; the largest excess after a rub fell from 0.0033 to 3e-8 (float32). bear: a tip raises polish only where it leaves wax (blender or white pencil over 6B/charcoal/pastel left up to 305 waxless pixels polished up to 0.99; now none), and where a tip that does not melt drags wax off, polish goes with it (0.050 worst in the thorough suite; now none). A melting tip still polishes thin film beyond WAX_FAST, by design. 4 fingerprint drawings and colour.png (15 px by one level) change; rubs at most ~3% slower, within spread.

title: firmness(0.4) is not exactly 0, and leaves a denormal in the press arrays
description: In floating point 0.4 - 0.6 > -0.2, so a bearing of exactly 0.4 gives a firmness of about 7e-33 where the onset of burnishing should give none, and that can end as a denormal in crush or polish (was press). Harmless to the picture, but denormals are slow in the kernels, and the onset is not where it is said to be by one bit. Older than the rework of press; found doing it.
close_reason: firmness returns 0 at and below BURNISH_ONSET = 0.4, a constant written out (0.6 - 0.2 rounds to 0.39999999999999997, so it can't serve as the threshold). Picture unchanged: fingerprints identical, every example regenerated byte for byte.

title: Kernel loops that touch only float32 arrays are compiled 512 bits wide on AVX-512 machines, which costs a rub about a tenth
description: On a Xeon with AVX-512, LLVM compiles the loops of rub_under that touch only the sheet's float32 layers (press, stir, the slip of push_along) with zmm registers, and the others 256 bits wide. A do-nothing store that keeps those three loops at 256 bits makes a finger rub 0.91 and a stump rub 0.85 to 0.87 of its time (best of 15, interleaved, bit for bit the same result), and compiled for a processor without AVX-512 (NUMBA_CPU_NAME=haswell) the difference is gone. Why the wide loops are slower is not established (no performance counters on the machine: frequency licence, or 8-float loads over 4-float stores not being forwarded). press_dust is shared with bear, so strokes may pay the same: not measured. To do: measure strokes and rubs compiled for both; if the cost is real, find a documented way to keep the loops narrow (only options that numba documents: a target CPU or feature set for the kernels, not a trick store), or accept it. And any timing comparison on an AVX-512 host should be repeated with NUMBA_CPU_NAME=haswell: this nearly gave fusain-czc a false gain.
close_reason: Measured on an Emerald Rapids host, four interleaved best-of-15 runs. Compiled without AVX-512 (NUMBA_CPU_FEATURES = host features plus ,-avx512f, or real haswell), shading takes about 0.95 of its time, a finger rub 0.94, a stump rub 0.88, a kneaded-eraser rub 1.04; pens and render unchanged; every thorough fingerprint identical. The issue's comparison was invalid: NUMBA_CPU_NAME=haswell alone keeps the host's AVX-512 features (native vs that: 0.994). benchmark.py --cpu now empties NUMBA_CPU_FEATURES. Numba documents no per-function target CPU, only process-wide environment variables, which a library import should not set (intrusive, and silently ignored once numba is loaded): the README says how, and the cost is otherwise accepted.

The benchmark could do that itself (time.process_time, a --against of a saved run or of another checkout, best of N with the spread shown), and include a workload with flat ends, which it has none of.

title: hatching.strokes: a stub at a corner of the area wanders as far as a long stroke, and bends through a right angle
description: A stroke of a shading that is cut short by a corner of the area is kept if it is at least half a width long, and gets three knots that each wander 0.1 x width x hand, whatever its length. A stub 3 to 5 px long of a tip 8 wide is so bent through about a right angle and runs largely across the hatching's direction. The wander should probably go with the stroke's length. These stubs are the only strokes of the fingerprint suite where a flat end meets a hook shorter than half the tip (the seven --thorough drawings that fusain-hay changed). Found doing fusain-hay; not measured beyond those.
close_reason: A stroke's wander is capped at WANDER_SHARE = 0.05 of its own length (strokes of two tips or more unchanged; same draws). Stubs 6-12 px long: largest turn from the hatching direction 180° -> 35°, p95 130° -> 18°. 12 of 13 fingerprint drawings and 9 example images change (316 of 2623 strokes of the suite are stubs).

title: make pre-push fails in a fresh clone or worktree: tox's spell env needs cspell before anything installs it
description: pre-push runs tox first, and tox's spell env calls npm run spell, but node_modules/.bin/cspell is a prerequisite only of the spell and spell-changed targets of the Makefile. In a fresh clone or git worktree, make pre-push therefore stops at tox with 'cspell: not found' (exit 127) until npm install or npm ci has been run by hand. Making tox (or pre-push) depend on node_modules/.bin/cspell would fix it. Found by two lanes of the pass of 15 November 2026, each in its own worktree.
close_reason: The tox target of the Makefile has node_modules/.bin/cspell as a prerequisite, so make tox and make pre-push install cspell before tox's spell environment needs it. In a fresh clone tox -e spell failed with 'cspell: not found' (exit 127) and passes after the prerequisite is made. A git worktree under a checkout that has node_modules does not show the fault: npm run finds cspell through the parent directory.

title: Sheet.shade with a Stick: how many numbers it draws depends on the stick's wear, so on the pressure of what was drawn before
description: Sheet.shade takes its width from medium.width, which for a Stick follows the wear of its tip; the wear follows what earlier strokes laid, which follows their pressure. The width sets the default spacing, so the number of strokes of the shading and the number of draws hatching.strokes makes from the sheet's generator. A pressure field that wears a stick a little more or less therefore changes how many numbers later shades draw, and the grain of every mark after them: the sensitivity fusain-2n6 took out of Sheet.rub, by another path. A worn stick does cover differently, so the strokes may have to differ; what need not is the sheet's sequence after the shading (one draw for the shading, the strokes' numbers derived from it, as a rub's runs now are). Found doing fusain-2n6; not measured.
close_reason: Sheet.shade draws one number from the sheet (or takes seed=), the hand comes from a generator seeded with it and stroke k gets _seed_of(base, k), as a rub's stretches do: the sheet's sequence after a shading no longer follows the stick's wear. All 13 fingerprints and 10 example images change; nine test bounds that held for one sample were widened to the spread measured over several sheets.

title: A rub goes over each pixel's dust five times
description: In rub_under, lift, lay, spread, press in and stir each loop over the 27 numbers of one to three layers at a pixel. Working out the shares from the volumes first and applying them in one pass over the parts might be exact, since each part's operations do not depend on another's. Not measured; it would cost readability in rub_under, and must keep tools/refcounts.py clean and the fingerprints identical. A finger rub is 2.4 s and a stump rub 3.3 s on the benchmark's sheet after fusain-95m.
close_reason: Tried, and it stays as it is. The loops over a pixel's parts are a real share of a rub (about 42% of the kernel for a finger, 47% for a stump, 25% for a kneaded eraser), but one pass does not win them back: the layers are float32 and the arithmetic float64, so to be exact one pass must round at every step's store and saves loads and stores, no arithmetic, and LLVM if-converts it, working out every step for every part. Kernel time against the code as it is, best / median of 15 interleaved: one pass 1.08/1.10 (finger), 0.98/1.01 (stump), 1.35/1.37 (eraser). Fusing only spread+press+stir and push_along's two loops: 0.93/0.96, 0.90/0.90, 1.07/1.07 compiled with AVX-512, and 1.14, 1.06, 1.08 compiled without (NUMBA_CPU_NAME=haswell): its gain is only that it happens to keep loops at 256 bits that LLVM otherwise makes 512 bits wide. Every variant was bit for bit. rub_under's docstring says so.

title: A short stroke is 40% Python around the kernel
description: Sheet.stroke spends about 85 microseconds per call outside the kernel: murex's path sampling, three profiles, building arrays, and dispatching 19 arrays to numba. For the benchmark's 2000 short strokes that is 0.17 s of 0.43 s. Batching or caching the per-stroke arrays would help drawings made of many short strokes (hatching, examples/stilllife.py; see also fusain-6z7). Must stay byte-identical.
close_reason: A pressure, width or tilt given as a number is made an array at once (_along) instead of going through murex's profile evaluation, and the tip's shape array is filled column by column: around the kernel a short stroke takes 95 to 75 microseconds (CPU, kernel replaced by a no-op), 2000 short strokes 0.55 to 0.50 s; identical to the bit (thorough fingerprint, every example). What is left is mostly murex's path sampling, about 33 microseconds: a compiled resampling bit-exact with linspace and interp (8-10), a sample without the tangents fusain discards (1), one compiled call for the dense points (a few); perhaps 15 in all, 7% of a short stroke, and a change to spline's results is breaking for oilpaint. Handing the kernel its 19 arguments costs 1.3 microseconds: not worth a change.

title: A film of graphite on dust does not shine
description: Sheet.shine("graphite") counts only what the paper holds. Since fusain-wo4 a pencil drawn over a bed of dust lies on it as a film in the two layers, and that graphite has no sheen.
close_reason: Sheet.shine('graphite') and the render under a lamp now count the film a pencil lays on a bed of dust (_engine.film_sheen): the film is taken to hold the pencils' binding (0.85) of the graphite in its layer, never more than its own volume; on top it shines through all the matte of its layer, buried through its crumbs' clay and the matte above; with wax at the pixel it is taken for a wax film. Over two layers of pale soft pastel a 2B, 6B and HB line at 1.0 shine 0.88 to 0.90 of what they do on bare paper (0.001 to 0.003 before). A light line errs matte (2B at 0.3: a third), and a layer being one mixture (fusain-r56) is why.

title: melts of a coloured pencil ignores its softness
description: pencils.melts_of uses only the colour (how pale it is: white 0.75, cream 0.54, strong colours 0), and Medium.with_(softness=...) does not change it. A soft, waxy core should burnish more than a hard one of the same colour. The paleness rule, the stain thickness (STAIN), the smear of wax under an eraser (WAX_DRAG, DRAG_LAY) and WAX_FAST were assumed, not measured. Found doing fusain-d6p.

title: One press per pixel: the crush of a dry tip under or over wax goes with the wax, and thin wax polished flat keeps some press after it is erased
description: The cost of keeping one press per pixel (fusain-6k1 tells wax's polish from a dry tip's crush by whether the pixel holds wax). A hard lead pressed under coloured pencil, then erased, gets its tooth back. And where press exceeds what wax thinner than WAX_FAST holds up, the excess stays when the wax goes (a blender pressed hard over a very light layer). Storing the two apart would cost a float32 per pixel (about 1%) and an argument through lay_stroke, slide_on, put_down and bear.
close_reason: Two presses per pixel: Sheet.crush, the paper's own, raised by a dry tip pressed firmly and given back only by a tool that cuts the paper; Sheet.polish, the wax's, raised by any tip pressed firmly on wax and gone with the wax (polish <= wax / covered / WAX_FAST where a tool takes wax). Sheet.press is what a tip meets of the two (crush + polish - crush*polish), read-only. A 4H pressed under coloured pencil and erased with vinyl keeps its crush to the bit (0.918; on main 0.048 was left), a light HB shaded there touches 0.94 of the pixels (0.69), and after a blender pressed hard over a very light layer is erased no pixel keeps polish beyond what its wax holds (21% did). Memory 376 to 380 bytes a pixel; strokes 2 to 3% slower for the array.

title: A sand eraser or a knife leaves the paper no rougher than fresh
description: Scraped paper has raised fibres and takes more pigment, blotchily. press cannot go below 0, so scraped paper is modelled as fresh at best. Found doing fusain-6k1.

title: Sheet.rub with an unsteady hand strays past the edge of its area, and a loaded tool leaves dust there
description: Since a loaded tool gives its dust to bare tooth (fusain-9zh), where the hand of Sheet.rub strays past the edge of a tone the tool dirties the bare paper: examples/output/crayons.png, third row. A hand that strays less at the ends for tools, or a note in the docs, would settle it.
close_reason: Sheet.rub lays its passes with hatching.passes, the hand of someone rubbing: the middle of the tool keeps half its width inside the outline, every pass runs from that line to that line, the outermost passes run along it, and where the tool meets the edge it strays no more than the wander, and only inwards; a pass is as strong where it turns as in its middle. Nothing is left outside the area (a stump reached 7 px past the ends and 5 past the sides, a finger 14 and 10, darkening the paper by up to 0.5-0.6 of its luminance; now exactly nothing). The cost: a round tool kept inside reaches the rows along a side only with its rim, so the outermost pixel there is rubbed 0.11 to 0.32 as much as the middle (0.71 to 0.90 before, when the tool hung a quarter of its width outside) and the rows are as the middle from 3 to 5 px in. Sheet.shade is untouched to the bit.

title: Shading with the side of a stick may leave stripes where the bands' ends overlap; two tests pass narrowly
description: Not verified by measurement. Since fusain-bqe, Sheet.shade lays the even bands of a flat stick side by side, and the rounded ends of neighbouring bands double up over about half the stick's thickness: measure the cross-profile of a side-of-stick shading to see whether the stripes show or are believable. Also since fusain-bqe and fusain-d7v two tests pass only narrowly and are worth re-pinning by what they mean: tests/test_pens.py, firm hatching (firm < 0.6 x light: 0.649 against 0.657), and tests/test_dust.py, the precondition that over 5% of the paper stays bare under the side of a vine stick (0.054).
close_reason: Measured: where the bands of a flat stick met, a natural hand left lines of bare paper (+10 to +20 L* under compressed charcoal and soft pastel, +2 to +9 vine), since it strayed by 0.15 of the band's length (and varied it by a tenth) where bands overlap by 0.45 of the thickness; ruled strokes doubled up in a dark line (-3 to -9). The hand now strays and varies by the stick's thickness: +2.5 at most. A faint dark line stays (-1 to -5 natural hand, -3 to -9 ruled): overlapping less evens pigment but leaves a dull line in polished wax (oil pastel 0.82 uneven), since polish goes by the firmest pass. Found on the way: the floor of a shallow groove bit as fresh paper in its valleys, so HB over light ballpoint laid 1.10 of bare; it now bites as a tooth flattened as far as it is deep (1.01). Tests pinned over several sheets: pens light/bare 1.008-1.018 and firm/light 0.51-0.55 < 0.6 with the grain held; dust bare share > 0.02 (0.036-0.071 over 20 sheets).

title: macaw.py: give each part of the drawing its own random generator
description: build() and every draw_* step of examples/macaw.py share one generator, and the first draws scatter feather tiles over the plumage that is seen. Any change to the model that hides or shows a few plumage pixels (feet, thighs, wing edge) reshuffles every later stroke of the picture, the head included: redoing the feet (fusain-58g) moved 99% of the drawn pixels. If each part were drawn from its own child generator (SeedSequence(SEED).spawn), a local change would stay local in the image. It reshuffles the picture once when introduced. Also left from fusain-58g, to the eye: the near outer hind toe sweeps a little like a strap, and the claws read as wedges more than hooks.
close_reason: Each part of the macaw draws from a stream of its own (SeedSequence(SEED).spawn), items whose count follows what is seen have keyed streams, strokes and feathers are sown pixel by pixel instead of by choice() over the weights, and every stroke, shade and erase has its own seed through the new seed= of Sheet.stroke, shade, smudge, erase and rub (a seeded mark draws nothing from the sheet's generator). Hiding 144 plumage pixels beside a foot moved 82.4% of the drawn pixels; with the example alone 60.1%; now 2.6%, three quarters of them within 150 px. The drawing is the same with other grain: mean luminance of the bird 0.2621 to 0.2613, blocks of 100 px differ by 0.0042 at the median. What the issue says of the hind toe and the claws is fusain-9vi's.

title: A partly polished tooth glints pixel by pixel under the default lamp
description: With the narrow lobe of wax gloss (fusain-5je), facets that face the halfway direction catch the full gloss: in two layers of crayon at 0.7, 1% of pixels gain over 6 L*, and a few up to about 10.
close_reason: Cleared by the rework of press (fusain-2z5), not by the lamp. The glints were peaks of the tooth polished all the way (11% of the pixels past 0.8, 38% under 0.2) whose facet leaned 3 to 4 degrees towards the default lamp, where the wax lobe is steep (0.45 of its peak against 0.21 for a level facet). Two layers of crayon #141416 at 0.7 on cartridge paper, seeds 1 to 3, point lamp: 1.44% of pixels over 6 L*, brightest 10.47, top 0.1% 8.73 before; 0%, 3.56, 2.68 now, with no peak polished past 0.66. A test pins it. The owner's accepted default, a lamp with a width, was built and measured and on 16 November 2026 the owner chose to drop it: LAMP_RADIUS = atan(7.5/50) (a shade 15 cm across at half a metre, 8.5 degrees), every lobe of shininess n spread to n' with 1/n' = 1/n + r*r/16 and its peak times n'/n (closed form, within 1% of the mean sampled over the lamp's disc). It took the brightest from 10.47 to 10.01 before the press rework and from 3.56 to 3.48 after, dims the wax gloss overhead to 0.90, the ink's bronze to 0.86 and graphite to 0.98, and would redraw twelve images by 1 to 5 levels. Only a source about 60 degrees across would have cleared the glints by itself, at more than half the gloss overhead.

title: The ink a ball would gather beyond the most it holds is simply not gathered
description: With a HeldPen, long hatchings keep the rim of the ball at its cap, and the conservation identity (drops on the paper plus ink on the ball = BALL_GATHER times the lines' ink) only holds below it. Acceptable but undocumented: document it, or model where the excess goes.
close_reason: Documented, not modelled: HeldPen, BALL_GATHER, roll_stroke, Sheet.stroke and docs/design.md say that the rim holds at most BALL_BLOB, that what the ball would gather beyond it goes nowhere, and that the conservation identity holds only while the rim has never been full (a clean 3-pixel pen fills it in 130 px at full pressure, 240 at 0.5, 360 at 0.3). A test pins the cap.

title: The macaw's feet are in an impossible posture
description: examples/macaw.py: the body and plumage are great, the face is fine and the beak passable; leave those. The feet are in a posture no parrot's could take and must be redrawn in a realistic pose: a macaw's foot is zygodactyl (two toes forward, two back), gripping the perch from both sides, the toes wrapping round it with the claws showing beneath, the legs short and coming down from under the belly feathers. Work from reference photographs of a perched macaw. Very low priority, but it needs doing at some point. Alters one picture: regenerate examples/output/macaw.png.
close_reason: The branch crosses under the bird and each foot closes round it: a short leg from under the thigh feathers, the hind toes curling down the near side with their claws hooking under, the forward toes over the top. Worked from anatomy (no photographs could be fetched). The rest of the bird is the same drawing with other strokes: the model's occlusion feeds the first random draws.
